The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

The discoveries build on the gardens' rich biodiversity and mark a new chapter for the museum's 5-acre (2-hectare) outdoor site, now transformed into a network of interconnected habitats, from chalk grasslands to woodlands, designed to support wildlife, engage visitors and advance scientific understanding of urban ecosystems.

Alongside traditional species surveys and visual observations, museum scientists are using pioneering techniques including environmental DNA (eDNA), acoustic monitoring and a growing network of environmental sensors. Together, these approaches are generating millions of records and opening up new ways to investigate how wildlife responds to changes in habitat, climate and human activity. The research is described in an article in The London Naturalist .

The gardens have a long history of biological recording, with 3,500 species documented since monitoring began in 1995. These include several arthropod species recorded for the first time in the U. K. , as well as numerous first regional records.

The Nature Discovery Garden now provides an opportunity to investigate biodiversity across a much larger and more varied area, from woodland and meadow habitats to ponds, planted areas and spaces designed to demonstrate climate-resilient gardening. The latest discoveries add to this extensive record and highlight the potential of urban green spaces to support biodiversity. Among the latest additions are:

Ed Baker, acoustic biology researcher at the Natural History Museum, said, "Recording 92 new species in our new gardens shows just how much wildlife can thrive in the heart of London. By combining traditional wildlife surveys with new technologies, we can better understand how urban nature responds to changes in climate, habitat and human activity—and how we can make our cities better places for both people and wildlife."

The mucus layer in the human gut is a tough place for bacteria: nutrients are scarce, and conditions are harsh. How do bacteria adapt to such extreme environments? Researchers at the Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI) and the Chair of Microbiology of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität (JMU) in Würzburg, working with scientists at Vanderbilt Health in the United States, have identified a key regulator.

They found a small RNA in the gut bacterium Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron that responds to iron and nutrient scarcity. The findings offer novel insights into how intestinal bacteria adapt and open up new possibilities for microbiome-based therapies. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications .

Trillions of bacteria live in the human gut. Many are beneficial: they aid digestion, produce vitamins and protect against pathogens. One of the most important groups is Bacteroides. These gut residents are masters at breaking down complex sugars that humans cannot digest on their own. But not all bacterial populations occupy the same region of the gut. Some live freely in the gut lumen, while others are embedded in the thick mucus layer covering the intestinal wall. The latter is an especially challenging environment, where nutrients and iron are scarce. Microorganisms must also adapt their surfaces and metabolism to attach to the mucus and survive.

"Understanding how bacteria colonize these habitats is a central question in microbiome research," says Alexander Westermann, professor at the Julius-Maximilians-Universität (JMU) and an affiliated scientist at the Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI). While proteins that regulate gene expression in the microbiota have been studied considerably, another class of regulators has recently attracted attention: small ribonucleic acids, or sRNAs.

These short RNA molecules do not encode proteins but act as post-transcriptional switches, allowing microbes to adjust their physiology rapidly. To understand a healthy microbiota, it is essential to grasp how commensal bacteria, such as B. thetaiotaomicron, use these molecules to colonize specific regions of the gut.

A team at HIRI—a site of the Braunschweig Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) in cooperation with the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU)—has now, together with scientists from Vanderbilt Health in Nashville, Tennessee, discovered a novel sRNA that regulates gene expression as the bacteria colonize the gut lining. The team named it IroR. It responds in particular to iron scarcity and to the availability of mucus as a carbon source.

To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity.

Simulating such processes on a computer is difficult. Quantum-mechanical calculations can be used to investigate where additional electrons prefer to reside and how they move, but these calculations are extremely computationally demanding. As a result, it is hardly possible to track these movements over longer periods of time.

One obvious idea is therefore to use machine learning: certain physical situations can be calculated in great detail, and the results can then be used to train an AI model. Ideally, the AI learns to make accurate predictions for other situations as well, without having to repeat the complete, extremely time-consuming calculations every time.

Unfortunately, it is not quite that simple. "Previous AI methods quickly reach their limits, especially when it comes to the movement of electrons within a material," says Michele Reticcioli from the Institute of Applied Physics at TU Wien.

"Sometimes they even produce clearly incorrect results that directly contradict our observations. In materials such as titanium oxide, for example, previous methods could not even correctly determine whether it is energetically favorable for an electron to become trapped at a particular atom."

This was precisely the problem with previous models. They had information about the positions of all the atoms, but not about which atoms were hosting additional, localized electrons. As a result, these models were unable to reliably predict the forces acting on the atomic scale.
Now, the team at TU Wien has succeeded in developing a method that overcomes this problem by combining several components into one powerful system. The study is published in the journal ACS Nano .

Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials .

Carbon dioxide, a climate-damaging waste gas from industrial processes, could serve as a valuable raw material. Using electricity, it can be converted into chemical feedstocks that are currently often produced from crude oil or natural gas. Catalysts facilitate the reaction and influence which products are formed. However, several substances can form simultaneously during CO₂ conversion. If unwanted hydrogen is produced, the electricity consumed in the process is no longer available to produce the desired product.

Dr. Pablo Lozano-Reis and professor Kai S. Exner from the University of Duisburg-Essen (UDE) have investigated how these processes can be controlled. Their research focuses on Ti₃C₂Tₓ, a material known as an MXene, composed of ultrathin atomic layers. It consists of titanium (Ti) and carbon (C), while Tₓ denotes atoms and groups of atoms on its surface, including oxygen.

The restructuring takes place in two steps: a positive voltage pulse, in combination with water, causes individual titanium atoms to protrude slightly from the surface. CO₂ can attach to neighboring oxygen atoms and react there, while hydrogen cannot form at these sites. A second voltage pulse with reversed polarity triggers further restructuring—but only if CO₂ itself is involved. In the process, carbon monoxide (CO) detaches from the surface, leaving a gap in the oxygen layer. This creates a new reaction site that yields a different mix of products.

"The substance we want to convert effectively helps shape its own reaction site," explains Exner. "By coordinating the voltage pulses, we can influence both the structure of the catalyst surface and the distribution of reaction products."

The calculations suggest that, of all the configurations investigated, the restructured surface is best suited to producing formic acid, a versatile chemical feedstock. However, if the second pulse is too strong, the surface becomes unstable and once again favors hydrogen formation.

Experiments, particularly those involving copper catalysts, have already shown that voltage pulses influence the products of CO₂ conversion. But what happens on the catalyst surface is difficult to observe experimentally. The simulations reveal these processes for Ti₃C₂Tₓ at the atomic level and provide insights into how catalysts and pulse sequences can be tailored to produce specific chemicals.

Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

Now, researchers at Tohoku University have developed a new approach that makes quantitative rock analysis more accessible. By combining a conventional polarizing microscope with a newly developed software tool called NicoNavi, the team enabled the measurement of the size, shape and crystallographic orientations of mineral grains using video recordings of rotating rock samples.
Details were published in the Journal of Petrology on Nov. 9, 2026.

The technique takes advantage of how minerals interact with polarized light. As a thin slice of rock rotates beneath the microscope, individual mineral grains change in brightness and color depending on their crystallographic orientations. By recording these changes through a full 360-degree rotation, the researchers can identify individual grains and their boundaries, then generate detailed maps of their microstructures.

NicoNavi brings these measurements together in a single workflow, including mineral classification and three-dimensional analysis of crystallographic c-axis orientations in suitable minerals such as quartz (silicon dioxide, SiO₂). With a few additional optical measurements, including a slight tilt of the sample, quartz c-axis analysis can be completed in approximately 10 minutes.

"One of the biggest advantages of this approach is that it makes quantitative analysis possible using equipment that is already available in many laboratories," says Dr. Tan Furukawa of Tohoku University's Graduate School of Science. "By combining relatively simple optical measurements with automated image analysis, we hope to make it easier for researchers to collect and compare large amounts of information about the internal structures of rocks."

To assess the accuracy of their approach, Furukawa and professor Tatsuki Tsujimori compared NicoNavi's results with those obtained using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), an established technique that measures crystal orientations using an electron microscope. For rock samples with thin sections approximately 20–35 micrometers thick, the two methods produced broadly consistent results for grain boundaries, grain statistics and c-axis orientation distributions.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes severe respiratory disease and is responsible for numerous deaths each year. A research team led by DZIF scientist Dr. Wendy K. Jo and DZIF scientist Dr. Jan Felix Drexler at Charité—University Medicine Berlin, as well as DZIF board member Dr. Thomas Pietschmann and Dr. Sibylle Haid from TWINCORE in Hanover, has now characterized a virus in West African fruit bats that is genetically distinct from known RSV variants but belongs to the same viral family as RSV.

The team was able to demonstrate that the pathogen can potentially be transmitted from animals to humans, but that our immune responses provide protection. Their findings have now been published in the journal Science Advances .

The aim of the study was to assess the epidemiology and zoonotic potential—that is, the transmissibility from animals to humans—of a bat RSV using multidisciplinary approaches. The study combines fieldwork with computer-based and laboratory experiments to examine epidemiology, genomic properties, treatment options, and host barriers—that is, biological obstacles which a pathogen must overcome to infect a host or to jump from one host species to another.

The team examined 1,778 bats from Ghana and Benin. The epidemiological data showed a low virus detection rate of 1. 4%. Antibodies against the virus were detected in 9% of the studied bats. A detailed analysis of the RSV genomes from two bats showed that the bat viruses are not closely related to human RSV. Experiments did, however, prove that bat RSV can enter human cells, albeit less efficiently than human RSV. The studies were conducted using a viral system that contains only a portion of the bat RSV proteins but still allows for comparison with human RSV.

"Bat RSV can inhibit the human innate immune response, the body's built-in first line of defense, but it is neutralized by antibodies from individuals who have previously been exposed to RSV. In addition, we show that a broadly effective monoclonal antibody can neutralize bat RSV," explains lead author Jo.

The study underscores that, in addition to genomic data, functional data are also necessary to characterize the properties of a virus in order to make well-founded assessments of its zoonotic risk potential. "The results show how important it is to investigate newly discovered viruses in animal reservoirs using various scientific methods in order to better gauge potential risks," comments Drexler.

Furthermore, the results support the development of broad-spectrum antiviral agents that are effective against various reservoir-associated viruses. The complex work carried out here was made possible by collaboration among DZIF sites with diverse areas of expertise. The next step will utilize a reverse genetics system to investigate how genetic changes can affect viral pathogenesis.

articles.title: Crowded Proteins Can Change How Enzymes Work
articles.dek: Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.
paragraphs: Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.

In laboratory droplets designed to mimic conditions inside cells, enzymes worked faster as the liquid became more crowded with proteins, up to a point. Active enzymes also helped nearby molecules move more freely through the liquid.

Many of the chemical reactions that keep cells alive occur in the cytoplasm, where proteins and other molecules can gather into compartments without an enclosing membrane. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) , in collaboration with the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization (MPI-DS) and RIKEN, studied how enzymes interact with these crowded environments.

“What’s fascinating is that we can connect interactions between individual atoms to the movement of molecules across an entire droplet. Events at the smallest scales can shape, and be shaped by, the physical behavior of a much larger system,” says senior author Professor Paola Laurino, who leads the Protein Engineering and Evolution Unit at OIST.

The OIST researchers prepared tiny droplets containing different concentrations of a protein called bovine serum albumin (BSA). In separate experiments, they introduced two enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), along with their substrates, the molecules upon which the enzymes act.
Enzyme activity increased as more BSA was added to the droplets. Only at very high protein concentrations did crowding begin to interfere with the reactions.

“This initial increase in enzymatic activity seemed counter-intuitive, as you’d typically expect any level of crowding to impair movement of the enzymes and substrates and increase the liquid’s viscosity, therefore slowing down the reaction from the start,” explains Laurino.

Laurino and her team also used fluorescent tracers to examine how enzyme activity affected the movement of molecules within the droplets. Both BSA proteins and fluorescent nanoparticles moved more freely in the presence of active enzymes. Droplets containing modified, inactive enzymes were more viscous, and molecules moved more slowly through them.

“Similarly, we found that higher concentrations of the enzymes or their substrates in the droplets also increased mobility,” says Professor Ramin Golestanian, director of the Department of Living Matter Physics at MPI-DS.
The researchers used fluorescent markers to track the movement of nanoparticles in the droplet. Credit: Dindo et al. , 2026, 10. 1038/s41467-026-77666-y.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted by researchers at RIKEN suggested that crowding helped accelerate reactions by changing the shape of the enzymes. The simulations showed that the active site, the region where substrates bind and react, was open under dilute conditions and closed as the concentration of surrounding proteins increased.

“When closed, the energy barrier required was much lower, allowing the reaction to happen more readily,” explains Laurino. “To detect such a change in these simulations by MD was really surprising to us.”

Researchers at MPI-DS developed a theoretical model to explain the increased movement within the droplets. They proposed that enzyme activity creates differences in chemical concentrations throughout the liquid, generating tiny flows.
“These flows allow the molecules to move more freely and mix within the droplet, highlighting how enzyme activity can potentially lead to physical effects across larger scales,” says Golestanian.

articles.title: Glaciers Are Melting at Alarmingly Different Rates and Climate Alone Can’t Explain Why
articles.dek: Where a glacier ends can influence how quickly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.
paragraphs: Where a glacier ends can influence how quickly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.

Between 2000 and 2020, the number of lakes in direct contact with glaciers worldwide grew by about 35 percent. Their expansion has consequences for the ice that remains. Lake water can melt glaciers from underneath, while chunks of ice can break away and fall into the water. Until recently, scientists had struggled to determine how much these processes contribute to glacier loss worldwide.

An international research team, including Tobias Bolch from the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), used artificial intelligence to map glacial lakes from satellite images taken in 2000 and 2020. The researchers manually checked the results, distinguishing lakes that touched glaciers from those already separated from the ice. Their findings were published in Nature Climate Change .

Over the 20-year period, glaciers ending in lakes lost an average of 66 centimeters (26 inches) of water equivalent annually, meaning the lost ice would produce a layer of water that deep. By comparison, glaciers ending on land lost 40 centimeters (16 inches), and those ending in the sea lost 36 centimeters (14 inches).

“Our research has shown that contact with a lake further accelerates the loss of ice from a glacier,” says Tobias Bolch. “While the climate and the topography of the glacier are the most significant factors influencing glacial mass loss, lakes significantly exacerbate it.”

The number of lakes touching glaciers increased by more than 3,500, with particularly pronounced expansion in Alaska and the southern Andes. Their combined area grew by around 600 square kilometers (232 square miles). They also gained an estimated 66 cubic kilometers of water, enough to submerge the entire city of Vienna under approximately 160 meters (525 feet) of water

Using machine learning models, the researchers found that glacier characteristics such as elevation and slope accounted for 46 percent of the explained influence on ice gains and losses. Temperature, precipitation, and other climatic factors accounted for around 43 percent, while glacial lakes contributed approximately 11 percent.

“The findings from this study will help us to estimate future changes to the glaciers more accurately,” says Tobias Bolch. “This is particularly important for mountainous regions and their forelands, where meltwater is a significant source of water. Such findings are also relevant when assessing the risks posed by glacial lakes in the event of potential outbursts.”

articles.title: Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory
articles.dek: Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.
paragraphs: Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.

In the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors. One of the apparent victims, an adult male baboon, was estimated to have weighed more than 26 kilograms (57 pounds), challenging a long-held assumption about the dangers early humans faced.

Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey. Scientists believed that humans and their ancestors had escaped this threat for roughly the past 2. 5 million years because they were too heavy for even the giant eagles of the past to lift.

The discovery comes from the Ennedi Plateau in northern Chad, where an isolated population of baboons lives in the Sahara Desert. Researchers from the University of St Andrews traveled to the region with colleagues from Dartmouth College, the University of Konstanz, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

Lead author Professor Catherine Hobaiter, from the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, said, “This was such an extraordinary expedition, any primatologists dream! Some of the baboons there are so remote they rarely, if ever, see people, and so after a couple of days they ended up following us around—we were probably the most interesting thing they’d seen for a while!”

She added: “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them. Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

In a new study published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology , the researchers describe finding the remains of adult male baboons with telltale signs of eagle predation, including talon punctures in their skulls and distinctive scrapes and rake marks on their shoulder bones.

Senior author Professor Nathaniel Dominy from Dartmouth College said, “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t. Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”
The behavior of the living baboons offered another clue.

Professor Hobaiter explained, “One of the most exciting observations was seeing the baboons respond when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles swept overhead—primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat. We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety.”

For scientists studying human evolution, the possibility of attacks from above is particularly interesting. Primates defend themselves differently against eagles than they do against predators such as big cats and crocodiles. One strategy, known as mobbing, involves primates, particularly larger adult males, charging an attacker to drive it away. If our ancestors faced similar threats, eagles may have helped shape the evolution of communication and group cooperation.

Many primates living in areas where eagles hunt also travel in large groups alongside other primate species. For much of our evolutionary history, our ancestors shared their surroundings with other early human species and primates. Although these relationships are often viewed in terms of competition, protection from predators may have given them a reason to stay together.

Dr. Gisela Kopp, from the University of Konstanz and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, said, “Primatology often focuses on regions with a high diversity of primates, but shifting our attention to a place where no primatological data has ever been collected before, proved to be extremely rewarding.”

Dr. Jean Didier Akpona, from African Parks, said, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence. This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”

articles.title: New Technology Could Help Astronauts Make Their Own Oxygen on the Moon
articles.dek: Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.
paragraphs: Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.
Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.
Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil .
This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.
But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.
Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.
So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well-established industrial technology called “plasma-processing.”

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid, and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.
In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process that underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?
To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.
The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.
Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

articles.title: Astronomers Discover the Sun Contains 55% More Silver Than Previously Thought
articles.dek: Some of the oldest rocks in the solar system hinted that astronomers were undercounting the Sun’s silver. A fresh look at sunlight suggests they were right.
paragraphs: Some of the oldest rocks in the solar system hinted that astronomers were undercounting the Sun’s silver. A fresh look at sunlight suggests they were right.
Researchers at Uppsala University estimate that silver is 55 percent more abundant in the Sun than previous calculations indicated.

The revised estimate brings the Sun much closer to the silver abundance found in primitive meteorites. Both preserve material from the same cloud of gas and dust that gave rise to the solar system 4. 6 billion years ago.

Silver atoms in the Sun’s atmosphere absorb light at specific wavelengths, leaving dark lines in the spectrum. The pattern identifies silver, but estimating how much is there requires a model that predicts how strongly those atoms absorb light.

The team modeled the motion of the Sun’s outer layers and used more detailed calculations of how silver atoms interact with light and other particles. The model accounts for how radiation changes the energy states of silver atoms, which affects the strength of the lines astronomers use to measure the element’s abundance.

“With our new model, we were able to interpret the spectral lines used to determine the solar silver abundance more accurately,” says Sema Caliskan, who conducted the research during her PhD studies at Uppsala University.

Hydrogen and helium make up nearly all of the Sun. Heavier elements such as carbon, iron, and silver account for just 1. 5 percent of its mass. Many of these elements form inside stars or during stellar explosions, then become part of later generations of stars and planets. Measuring their abundance helps astronomers reconstruct how the Milky Way’s chemistry changed over time.

“The new knowledge about the Sun’s composition is important for the understanding of other stars, planets, and cosmic material, because the Sun is one of astronomy’s key reference points,” says Caliskan.

The team plans to apply the same method to other stars. “By studying the light of stars of different types and ages, we hope to understand where silver is formed in the universe, and how it has been distributed throughout the Milky Way over time,” says Caliskan.

articles.title: A Black Hole Smaller Than an Atom Could Trigger One of the Universe’s Most Violent Explosions
articles.dek: An ancient black hole no larger than an atom could consume a star from within and eventually trigger a spectacular explosion.
paragraphs: An ancient black hole no larger than an atom could consume a star from within and eventually trigger a spectacular explosion. New simulations by physicists at MIT and collaborating institutions suggest that these events could produce detectable bursts of radiation, offering a possible way to discover black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang.
The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal , could also help scientists investigate dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Primordial black holes may have formed when exceptionally dense regions collapsed under gravity during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. The smallest would have evaporated through Hawking radiation, but heavier examples could survive today. Some might be as small as an atom yet contain the mass of an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

The researchers investigated what would happen if one of these black holes encountered a Sun-like star. Although a star’s gravity alone would not capture a passing black hole, interactions involving a companion star or planet could trap it. Repeated passages through the star would gradually reduce its orbital energy, allowing it to settle into the stellar core over thousands to millions of years.
“Then, this is where the action begins,” says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The team’s three-dimensional simulations suggest that a captured black hole could grow by consuming stellar material. Within several million years, it might absorb approximately 1 percent of the star’s mass. If the star rotates fast enough, the remaining gas would form a spinning disk around the black hole.
“Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,” Gottlieb says. “The black hole is also spinning, and it’s twisting space and time.”
As material spirals inward, the black hole would twist magnetic fields in the surrounding disk, generating powerful jets capable of tearing through the star.
“Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,” Gottlieb says.

“This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,” Gottlieb explains. “And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It’s very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.”

The resulting explosion could produce a brilliant flash of blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays. As the event evolves, its emissions would shift across the electromagnetic spectrum.

“We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,” Gottlieb says. “This is something we could potentially detect, if it’s not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.”

Other cosmic explosions can produce similar signals, so astronomers would need additional evidence to identify a primordial black hole. One possible clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not normally be expected to explode.

“For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside,” Gottlieb says.

articles.title: NASA’s NG-25 Mission to Launch Pioneering Space Crops Research
articles.dek: NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial…
paragraphs: NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency.
Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health.

Astronauts will need sustainable sources of food to travel farther and stay longer in space. To help understand how crop production works in microgravity, NASA is launching a novel space crops experiment .

The new prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing safe, nutritious, and reliable crop production systems for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Knowledge gained from the space crop production system also could help inform agricultural practices such as vertical farming and indoor growing systems.
Researchers will use this investigation to validate the system’s water delivery and volume optimization technology aboard the space station.
A precision health investigation is the next step toward enabling long-duration studies of human brain tissues in space.

The research builds on a previous investigation that sent small, lab-grown models of the human brain, called miBrains, to the space station. This experiment will validate a miniature fluid-handling system designed to mix, deliver, and maintain the nutrient-rich liquid needed to keep the tissues alive.

Researchers could use the findings to help identify potential neurological risks associated with spaceflight and develop strategies to protect astronaut health. It also may advance human tissue research and neurological disease modeling on Earth.

NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

articles.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
articles.dek: In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds.
paragraphs: In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.

The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5. 6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows .

In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano.

On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft . In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports , prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.

articles.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
articles.dek: In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats , brought to the country to control other nonnative animal…
paragraphs: In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats , brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”

So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō , and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park . This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “ landmark effort ,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

articles.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
articles.dek: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions…
paragraphs: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”
Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”
NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

articles.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
articles.dek: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from…
paragraphs: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.
Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.
Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.
The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.
Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.
Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

articles.title: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard
articles.dek: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
paragraphs: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.
When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”
As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U. S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”
The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

articles.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
articles.dek: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once…
paragraphs: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.
My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure . Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding , including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes . Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials .

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years . Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories .

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly . In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes .

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow .” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.
To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “ I’m not going to abandon my house . It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding , but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage . I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.
If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost , and some left .

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods . But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.
Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.
